content:
<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, Rep. John W. Mannion, Rep. Adelita S. Grijalva>: INTRODUCTION
H.R. 2555, the Freedom of Association in Higher Education Act, introduced by Rep. Erin Houchin (R-IN), amends the Higher Education Act of 1965 (HEA) to prohibit institutions of higher education (IHEs) that receive funding under title IV of HEA (Title IV) from preventing students from forming or applying to join a single-sex social organization. The bill also prohibits IHEs from taking adverse actions against students based solely on their membership in a single-sex organization. The Committee has considered legislation similar to H.R. 2555 over several Democratic and Republican-led Congresses. However, the markup of H.R. 2555 needlessly inserted a poison pill (specifically language to discriminate against transgender individuals) into an otherwise bipartisan bill. Until these provisions are removed, Committee Democrats cannot support this bill.
STUDENTS' RIGHTS TO FREELY ASSOCIATE HAVE BIPARTISAN SUPPORT
As introduced, H.R. 2555 stood for a simple proposition: institutions of higher education should not be able to take adverse actions against students simply for their decision to join fraternities, sororities, or other single-sex organizations. Language to amend HEA for this very purpose was included in comprehensive bills reauthorizing the HEA led by Republicans in the 115th Congress, and Democrats in the 116th Congress.\1\ Committee Democrats support the rights of college students to join fraternities, sororities, and other student organizations. Many Members of Congress are members of such organizations and some continue to participate as alumni members of such organizations.
\1\H.R. 4508 Sec. 119, 115th Cong. (2017); H.R. 4672 Sec. 1020, 116th Cong. (2019). In the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic the Committee did not consider a comprehensive HEA reauthorization in the 117th Congress, and in the 118th Congress, the Committee considered a non-comprehensive reauthorization bill focused on the cost of college.
TRANS-EXCLUSIONARY POLICIES ARE A MAJORITY POISON PILL
As introduced, H.R. 2555 was a bipartisan bill likely to garner widespread (if not unanimous) Committee support. However, the amendment in the nature of a substitute (ANS) offered during consideration of H.R. 2555 needlessly inserted partisan poison pills into the bill related to the exclusion of transgender students. Specifically, the ANS added definitions of ``sex'', ``male'', ``female'', and ``single-sex organization'' to the bill, denying the right to of transgender students to be protected under the bill.\2\ Based on the language of the ANS, single-sex organizations would be defined as groups composed of students based on their sex as assigned at birth, and would bar transgender students from joining single-sex organizations consistent with their gender identity.\3\
\2\The ANS' definitions are an attempt to limit the definition of ``sex'' in this section to mean biological sex at birth. However, the Supreme Court held in 2020 that, even when interpreting ``sex'' to mean biological sex at birth, certain instances of discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity require a prerequisite discrimination on the basis of biological sex at birth and as such are illegal under certain sex discrimination statutes. Bostock v. Clayton County, 590 U.S. 644, 660. Recent analysis by the Court, specifically in the Title IX context suggests this interpretation is still valid. See West Virginia v. B.P.J., 609 U.S. ___ (Gorsuch J. conc.) (``Bostock v. Clayton County supports, not undermines, the Court's conclusion.'') (internal citations omitted).
\3\Compare H.R. 2555, 119th Cong. (2025) (as introduced) (``Any student (or group of students) enrolled in an institution of higher education shall--(1) be able to form or apply to join any recognized or unrecognized social organization, including any single-sex social organization;'') with H.R. 2555, 119th Cong. (2025) (Amdt. in the Nature of a Substitute) (``Any student (or group of students) enrolled in an institution of higher education . . . shall--`(1) be able to form, apply to join, join, participate in, or lead a single-sex social organization of the student's sex . . .'') (emphasis added).
Prior to the ANS, there was no language in H.R. 2555 related to single-sex organizations and gender identity. Such language was not present in past iterations of the Freedom of Association in Higher Education Act considered as part of HEA reauthorizations by the Committee, or in the standalone version of the bill from previous Congresses introduced by Republican Members of the Committee.\4\ The narrow focus of the bill from its inception up until this markup was protecting students' rights to associate from university intrusion. Instead, the bill, as reported out of Committee, removes university intrusion but replaces it with congressional intrusion into students' rights to associate among themselves. Committee Democrats have seen nothing to suggest that the fraternal and sororal organizations that advocated for H.R. 2555 asked for this language to be added to the bill. This is consistent with the Majority's continued insistence on moving legislation through Committee that denies the existence of transgender students.
\4\See H.R. 4508 Sec. 119, 115th Cong. (2017); H.R. 4672 Sec. 1020, 116th Cong. (2019); H.R. 7488, 117th Cong. (2022).
The ANS essentially undermines H.R. 2555's entire rationale. Students either have the right to freely associate among themselves or they do not. By definition, part of that right involves letting students freely make decisions about the makeup of their organizations on their own.
During the markup, the Majority made mention of a sorority being sued based on its membership policy limiting its membership to cisgender women. It is clear there will be emerging legal questions regarding the right of single sex organizations to make membership decisions based on their member's sex assigned at birth. It is also clear that those questions will likely not be as clear cut as the Majority would like us to believe.\5\ Regardless, those questions are fundamentally different than and extraneous to the legal question the Freedom of Association in Higher Education Act was written to answer.
\5\See West Virginia v. B.P.J., 609 U.S. ___ (Gorsuch, J., conc.) (``Bostock v. Clayton County supports, not undermines, the Court's conclusion.'') (internal citations omitted); West Virginia v. B.P.J., 609 U.S. ____ (Op. of Sotomayor, J.,) (``Yet there are plenty of contexts outside of athletics in which Title IX applies and does not allow sex distinctions like this one to be drawn. Title IX does not allow schools, for example, to institute mandatory sex-segregated classes or extracurricular activities like chess club, theater, and student government.'')
DEMOCRATIC AMENDMENTS OFFERED DURING MARKUP OF H.R. 2555
At markup, Ranking Member Robert C. Bobby Scott (D-VA) put forward an amendment to strip the trans-exclusionary language from the bill. The amendment was defeated on a party-line vote.

exclusionary language
from the bill.
CONCLUSION
As introduced, H.R. 2555 had two bipartisan original co-sponsors. As a result of the adoption of the ANS, the lead Democrat co-sponsoring the bill, removed his support for the bill.\6\ It is clear from the ANS' adoption that Majority's obsession with making the world harder for transgender students wherever possible is more important than delivering long-sought bipartisan policy solutions. For the reasons stated above, all Committee Democrats present opposed H.R. 2555 when the Committee on Education and Workforce considered it on June 25, 2026. Unless the trans-exclusionary language is removed from the bill, we urge the House of Representatives to do the same.
\6\172 Cong. Rec. 107, H4252 (June 25, 2026) (statement of Rep. Garcia of California).
Robert C. ``Bobby'' Scott,
